expectedText:
CORPORATE BOARD RESOLUTION / ACTION BY WRITTEN CONSENT
Prepared for Acme, Inc.

WRITTEN CONSENT HEADING
Action by Unanimous Written Consent of the Board of Directors of Acme, Inc., in Lieu of a Meeting

The undersigned, being all of the directors of Acme, Inc., a corporation organized under the laws of California, presently serving on the board and constituting a quorum, do hereby consent in writing to the adoption of the following resolution(s) without a meeting, effective as of September 1, 2026.

RESOLUTION TEXT
RESOLVED, that the Corporation is authorized to open a bank account at Acme Bank; and it is further

RESOLVED, that any officer of Acme, Inc. is authorized to take any further action necessary or appropriate to carry out the foregoing resolution.

This consent may be executed in counterparts, each of which is deemed an original, and all of which together constitute one instrument. This consent, and any counterparts, shall be filed with the minutes of the proceedings of the board of Acme, Inc.

BOARD ACTION WITHOUT A MEETING
A corporation's board of directors can take action without holding a meeting at all, but the bar for doing so is higher than at a meeting: every director then serving must individually or collectively consent in writing to the specific action, and the number of directors serving at the time must be enough to constitute a quorum. A meeting only needs a majority of directors present to vote yes; written consent in place of a meeting needs all of them to sign. The signed consent (or consents) must be filed with the minutes of the board's proceedings, the same as if the action had been taken at an actual meeting.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "An action required or permitted to be taken by the board may be taken without a meeting, if all members of the board shall individually or collectively consent in writing to that action and if the number of members of the board serving at the time constitutes a quorum. The written consent or consents shall be filed with the minutes of the proceedings of the board."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 307(b) (California Legislative Information text), California General Corporation Law, board action without a meeting requires unanimous written consent (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=307.)
  "This section applies also to committees of the board and incorporators and action by those committees and incorporators, mutatis mutandis."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 307(c) (California Legislative Information text), California General Corporation Law, meeting and written-consent rules extend to board committees and incorporators (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=307.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a genuine formal requirement — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific corporation. The statute contains a specific carve-out for an “interested director” or “common director” (as those terms are defined in a separate conflict-of-interest statute, Section 310): such a director can be counted among “all members of the board” for unanimity purposes by abstaining in writing from the consent, if the required conflict-of-interest disclosures were made first and are included in the consent — a real but narrow exception this clause does not attempt to fully restate. Both citations below are subsections of the same statutory section (§ 307) rather than independently authored sources; no additional independent source was found for this.

THE MEETING ALTERNATIVE: NOTICE AND WAIVER
A board can also act the traditional way, at a meeting, rather than by written consent. A regular meeting needs no notice at all if its time and place were already fixed by the bylaws or the board. A special meeting is different — it requires at least four days' notice by mail, or 48 hours' notice delivered personally, by telephone (including voicemail), or electronically — and the articles or bylaws cannot eliminate that requirement. But a director can waive that notice: by signing a written waiver, a written consent to holding the meeting, or a written approval of the minutes afterward, or simply by attending the meeting without objecting, before or at its start, to the lack of notice. Any such waiver, consent, or approval has to be filed with the corporate records or made part of the meeting minutes.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "Regular meetings of the board may be held without notice if the time and place of the meetings are fixed by the bylaws or the board. Special meetings of the board shall be held upon four days’ notice by mail or 48 hours’ notice delivered personally or by telephone, including a voice messaging system or by electronic transmission by the corporation (Section 20). The articles or bylaws may not dispense with notice of a special meeting."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 307(a)(2) (California Legislative Information text), California General Corporation Law, notice for regular vs. special board meetings (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=307.)
  "Notice of a meeting need not be given to a director who provides a waiver of notice or a consent to holding the meeting or an approval of the minutes thereof in writing, whether before or after the meeting, or who attends the meeting without protesting, prior thereto or at its commencement, the lack of notice to that director. These waivers, consents and approvals shall be filed with the corporate records or made a part of the minutes of the meeting."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 307(a)(3) (California Legislative Information text), California General Corporation Law, how notice of a board meeting is waived (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=307.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a genuine formal requirement — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific corporation. Both citations below are subsections of the same statutory section (§ 307) rather than independently authored sources; no additional independent source was found for this. Note for anyone tracing this research: an early research plan for this document guessed the notice requirement might live in § 311 and the waiver mechanism in § 307(a)(8). Both guesses were wrong when checked against the actual statute — § 311 turns out to govern board committees and their authority (see the companion clause on committee delegation), and the waiver mechanism is actually § 307(a)(3), not (a)(8) (which instead sets the majority-vote rule for acts done at a meeting).

WHY WRITTEN CONSENT NEEDS MORE SIGNATURES THAN A MEETING VOTE
There's a real structural gap, under this state's corporate law, between what it takes to skip a board meeting and what it takes to skip a shareholder meeting. Board written consent has no lesser-vote option at all — the statute requires every director then serving to sign, full stop, with no stated mechanism for the articles or bylaws to authorize anything less. Shareholder written consent, by contrast, generally only needs signatures from shareholders holding at least the number of votes that action would need to pass at a fully-attended meeting — which, for an ordinary majority-vote matter, is a majority of the outstanding voting shares, not every share. The one place shareholder written consent does require true unanimity is electing directors, which cannot be done by written consent at all unless every share entitled to vote on it signs on (subject to a narrow exception for filling a vacancy other than one created by removal).

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "An action required or permitted to be taken by the board may be taken without a meeting, if all members of the board shall individually or collectively consent in writing to that action and if the number of members of the board serving at the time constitutes a quorum."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 307(b) (California Legislative Information text), California General Corporation Law, board written consent requires every director serving to sign (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=307.)
  "Unless otherwise provided in the articles, any action that may be taken at any annual or special meeting of shareholders may be taken without a meeting and without prior notice, if a consent in writing, as specified in Section 195, setting forth the action so taken, shall be provided by the holders of outstanding shares having not less than the minimum number of votes that would be necessary to authorize or take that action at a meeting at which all shares entitled to vote thereon were present and voted."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 603(a) (California Legislative Information text), California General Corporation Law, shareholder written consent needs only a meeting-equivalent vote count, not unanimity (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=603.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a genuine structural feature of its corporate law — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific corporation, and not a claim about how any other state's law treats written consent. An initial research plan for this document assumed that this state's default rule requires unanimity for both board AND shareholder written consent, by analogy to how some other states are commonly described as treating the two differently. On direct review of the actual statutory text, that assumption held for board consent but did not hold for shareholder consent generally — only the director-election consent is truly unanimous; other shareholder action by written consent uses the same vote count that would carry at a meeting, which is often well short of unanimous. This clause does not attempt to verify or characterize any other state's statute, and no comparison to another state's law is made or implied.

NOTICE AND REVOCATION AROUND A SHAREHOLDER WRITTEN CONSENT
When shareholders act by written consent instead of a meeting, two mechanical rules apply on top of the vote-count requirement itself. First, unless literally every shareholder entitled to vote signed the consent, shareholders who didn't sign are entitled to notice afterward that the action was taken — prompt notice for most actions, but at least 10 days before the action is carried out for a defined set of more sensitive actions (including certain conflict-of-interest approvals, indemnification approvals, and reorganizations). Second, a shareholder who signs a written consent can revoke it, but only up until the point enough consents to actually authorize the action have been filed with the corporation's secretary — not after.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "Unless the consents of all shareholders entitled to vote have been solicited in writing, both of the following shall apply: ... (2) Prompt notice shall be given of the taking of any other corporate action approved by shareholders without a meeting by less than unanimous written consent, to those shareholders entitled to vote who have not consented in writing. Notice shall be given as provided in subdivision (b) of Section 601."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 603(b) (California Legislative Information text), California General Corporation Law, notice to shareholders who didn't sign a written consent (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=603.)
  "Any shareholder giving a written consent, or the shareholder’s proxyholders, or a transferee of the shares or a personal representative of the shareholder or their respective proxyholders, may revoke the consent personally or by proxy by a writing received by the corporation prior to the time that written consents of the number of shares required to authorize the proposed action have been filed with the secretary of the corporation, but may not do so thereafter. The revocation is effective upon its receipt by the secretary of the corporation."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 603(c) (California Legislative Information text), California General Corporation Law, revoking a written consent (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=603.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a genuine formal requirement — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific corporation. Both citations below are subsections of the same statutory section (§ 603) rather than independently authored sources; no additional independent source was found for this. This document's authority clause on the general shareholder written-consent vote-count rule and the director-election unanimity exception (§ 603(a) and (d)) already appears elsewhere in this collection, in the Corporate Bylaws document's “Acting Without a Meeting” clause; this clause instead covers the two mechanical points — post-consent notice and revocation — that clause's own gap note flagged but did not cite.

DELEGATING BOARD AUTHORITY TO A COMMITTEE
A board of directors can, by resolution passed by a majority of the authorized number of directors, create a committee of two or more directors and give it some or all of the board's own authority to act — including, by the same logic as board action generally, the ability for that committee to act by the committee members' unanimous written consent instead of a meeting. That delegation has real, fixed limits: a committee can never approve anything that itself requires shareholder approval, fill a board or committee vacancy, set director compensation, adopt or amend bylaws, amend an unamendable board resolution, authorize a distribution outside board-set parameters, or appoint other committees.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "The board may, by resolution adopted by a majority of the authorized number of directors, designate one or more committees, each consisting of two or more directors, to serve at the pleasure of the board. ... Any such committee, to the extent provided in the resolution of the board or in the bylaws, shall have all the authority of the board, except with respect to: (a) The approval of any action for which this division also requires shareholders’ approval (Section 153) or approval of the outstanding shares (Section 152)."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 311 (California Legislative Information text), California General Corporation Law, board committees and the limits on delegated authority (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=311.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a genuine formal requirement — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific corporation. No additional independent source was found restating this specific committee-authority boundary. An earlier research plan for this document assumed this statutory section dealt with notice of board meetings; on direct review of the statutory text, that assumption was wrong — this section governs the scope of authority a board may delegate to a committee, not meeting notice (which is instead § 307(a)(2), covered in the companion clause on the meeting alternative).

DIRECTOR SIGNATURES
The undersigned directors of Acme, Inc. — Jordan Alex Lee, Morgan Lee — each sign below to evidence their unanimous written consent:

Director: _______________________ Date: _______________
Director: _______________________ Date: _______________
(Every director then serving must sign for this consent to be effective in place of a meeting. Add additional signature lines as needed.)
